chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
title: Jane Pittman question; Booker's cruel father
summary: Hinton asks about Miss Jane Pittman; Budd describes Pittman senior as a scandal-sheet publisher who beat his son.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: That sounds very reasonable, Budd. Also, I want to mention this thing here to you too, and ask you what's your opinion of it. Booker -- his wife's name was Pittman?
Well his wife's name was Pittman because she married him, but --
She married -- she married a man named Pittman, and he was a contractor.

Would you think that that would have anything to do then with the television show last season, Cicely Tyson, here recently, was a great television show about the saga of a life of Miss Jane Pittman. Was on television.
Oh, oh, Jane Pittman. Jane Pittman.
I wonder if it had any connection with this Pittman. [Film based on The Autobiography of Miss Jane Pittman, a novel by Ernest Gaines.]
I don't know. I can say this, her

husband was what you might call three-quarter mulatto, you know, he was very fat, had good hair, and he was a very smart man. Everybody hated him. He had a little publication that he used to put out called The Brotherhood Eyes, and he would scamper around and he had his different eyes, and whatnot, and he would get up -- he had a scandal sheet they used to print on the church women, and everything, and then bribed them and everything.

He was a sort of a scoundrel. In fact, when his young son, Booker Pittman, grew up, as I said, we were raised together, Booker used to say, "Come on, go home with me, man." I say, "What for?" He says, "My old man jumped on me, and I'm going to whip -- I'm going to fight him." And I said, "Okay." So me, like a damn' fool, so like after school we went to high school together and everything, you know, after school I'd go home with Booker, we'd be picking up bricks and stones and everything, and of course I was a little chicken, but I mean he was my friend, so I went along with him.

And when he would get to the house he would start humming bricks through the window, breaking panes, whizroom, blay-lay-lay-lay whrrrr, bam, bam, bam. Then they'd -- cause he was going to fight his old man. His old man used to fight him, like he was fighting a stranger. He'd fight him -- he whupped the kids with his fists. He never used a strap. He used to beat the hell out of them with his fists. He was a

mean man. You know?
And they used to fight like cats and dogs. Now Booker's mother was a very kind, beautiful woman, and as I told you, she was our music instructor at high school, and she allowed us to even drink.
